**Shellshock — the flaw in the shell itself (2014)**

On 12 September 2014 Stéphane Chazelas told Bash's maintainer that the shell had a serious flaw; it was disclosed on 24 September, once patches were ready. Bash passes functions to child processes by storing them in environment variables, and it kept on executing anything appended after the function definition. A variable set to `() { :; }; <command>` did not merely define an empty function — it ran the command too. The behaviour had sat in the code since 1989.

Bash is not only typed at. Web servers running CGI scripts copy request headers into environment variables before invoking a shell, so an attacker could put the payload in an ordinary `User-Agent` header and have the target's shell run their command with the web server's privileges. No login, no password. CISA issued an alert; live exploits appeared within hours of disclosure, and security firms recorded millions of probes in the days that followed.

Defenders found it in text. The attack left a literal signature in access logs — `() { :; };` sitting in a `User-Agent` or `Referer` field — so a single pass of `grep` over `/var/log` told an administrator whether they had been probed, and from where.

This lesson's tools are that story in miniature. Permission bits decide what a compromised web-server process can reach; pipes and `grep` turn a million log lines into the handful that matter; and "never let untrusted input reach a shell" becomes the reason a twenty-five-year-old convenience turned into a global emergency. The command line is where security work is done because it is also where a great deal of security goes wrong.

**Pakistan Telecom — the announcement that took YouTube off the internet (2008)**

On 24 February 2008, under a government order to block YouTube inside the country, Pakistan Telecom announced a route for the address block `208.65.153.0/24` — a slice of YouTube's address space — intending it to stay local. The announcement leaked to its upstream provider, PCCW, which passed it on, and routers around the world accepted it.

They accepted it because that is how networks find each other. Each network tells its neighbours which ranges of IP addresses it can deliver to, and where two announcements overlap the more specific one wins. YouTube was announcing the wider `208.65.152.0/22`; Pakistan Telecom's narrower `/24` was preferred over it. Packets for those servers were then carried, efficiently and correctly, to Pakistan, and discarded. The RIPE NCC's case study puts the start at 18:47 UTC and PCCW's withdrawal at 21:01 UTC; for much of the world YouTube was unreachable for around two hours.

Nothing was hacked. No password was stolen, no server was touched, and DNS returned the correct IP address throughout. What failed was the step in between: routing has historically taken each network's word for which addresses belong to it, in the same spirit that IP does not authenticate the sender of a packet.

This is why the request lifecycle is worth tracing rather than assuming. A name becomes an address, an address becomes a route, a route delivers you to a port, and only then does a handshake begin — four separate promises, each breakable on its own. Knowing the chain is what lets you say whether a failed connection is a bad DNS answer, a routing problem or a closed port.

**Spotify — the username that was two usernames (2013)**

Spotify allowed Unicode usernames — the character set reaching far beyond ASCII's 128 characters. To decide whether two names were the same it *canonicalised* them, folding look-alike characters down to one agreed form: the small-capital string `ᴮᴵᴳᴮᴵᴿᴰ` folds towards `bigbird`. Canonicalisation is meant to be idempotent: running it twice must give what running it once gave.

In the library Spotify used, it was not. For some characters a second pass produced a different string from the first, and Spotify's engineering write-up of June 2013 describes the consequence. Register an account under the odd-looking name, ask for a password reset, and the extra round of canonicalisation along that path landed the request on a different, existing account, resetting someone else's password. It was reported on Spotify's support forum by a user who, when doubted, took over the forum manager's account in minutes. The fix was to run the routine twice and reject any username whose results disagreed.

The underlying fact is the one this lesson opens with: characters are numbers. `A` is 65, `0x41`, `01000001`. Unicode numbers tens of thousands more, including many a human reads as identical. Two byte sequences can look the same on screen; two that look different can become the same after processing.

When a security decision compares text — a username, a filename, a blocked keyword — the question is never what it looks like. It is what bytes are there, what transformation runs before the comparison, and whether it runs the same number of times on every path. That is why analysts decode a hex dump or a Base64 blob before judging it.

**The Venona project — the one-time pad that was used twice (1943–1980)**

Soviet cable traffic in the 1940s was protected in two stages. A code book turned words into numeric groups, and those numbers were combined with digits drawn from a one-time pad using non-carrying addition — the arithmetic where 8 + 6 = 4, the carry thrown away. That is modular arithmetic doing the job this lesson describes: if the key digits are truly random and used once, the result is unbreakable.

The randomness held. The "used once" did not. Under pressure from the German advance on Moscow in late 1941, the organisation printing the pads produced around 35,000 pages of duplicate key, and wartime traffic pushed clerks into reissuing them. Reuse is fatal for a reason that is pure arithmetic: subtract two messages enciphered with the same key and the key cancels out, leaving a relationship between the two original texts, attackable with language statistics and patience.

The American effort began in February 1943, and the analyst Meredith Gardner broke into the code book in December 1946. Over the following decades they read roughly 2,900 messages, many only in fragments, before the project closed in October 1980. It was enough to identify Soviet agents including Klaus Fuchs and Julius Rosenberg.

The binary version is on your screen in this lesson. XOR is its own inverse, so `a ⊕ k ⊕ k = a` makes it a cipher — and that same property means two messages sharing one key satisfy `c₁ ⊕ c₂ = p₁ ⊕ p₂`, with the key gone. Repeated-key XOR is among the first things you will be asked to break, and no toy: the maths was never the weak part of a one-time pad — the discipline of never repeating the key was.

**Codecov — the build script that read everyone's environment (2021)**

Codecov's Bash Uploader was a small script that build pipelines downloaded and ran on every commit to report test coverage. On 31 January 2021 an attacker obtained a credential through a flaw in how Codecov built its Docker images, and used it to modify the copy of that script being served. The change was one line's worth of intent: as well as uploading coverage data, the script copied the build environment to a server the attacker controlled.

What lived in that environment was exactly what good practice puts there: the API keys and tokens developers had correctly kept out of their source code. The tampering ran undetected for two months, until on 1 April a customer compared the SHA-256 hash of the downloaded script against the value Codecov published, and found it did not match. Codecov's April 2021 post-mortem set out the timeline; Rapid7, HashiCorp and Twilio published their own. The only safe response was to rotate every credential the pipeline had seen.

Read the chain carefully: it is not the usual one. No secret was committed to a repository. The discipline this lesson teaches held. The secrets leaked anyway, because a script fetched from the internet at build time was trusted to do only what it said it did.

So take two rules from this lesson rather than one. Keep secrets out of Git — public repositories are scraped within minutes, and Git remembers a deleted secret for ever. Then keep going: the environment is a room, not a vault, and everything running in it can read it. Verify what you download against a published hash, and give any credential a pipeline holds the narrowest scope you can.
